en: Regarding the *Huayan Lun-guan* (The Thread of the Avatamsaka) by Master Furan:
Six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, who read all the worldly texts at once.

Having resolved his mind on enlightenment, he entered the Dragon Palace to examine the scriptural treasury (*pitaka*), where he saw that the *Avatamsaka* existed in three versions: the Upper, the Middle, and the Lower. The Upper version...

The original version contained verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousandfold world-systems, arranged in chapters numbering as many as the atoms in a four-continent world-system, totaling four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses in one thousand two hundred chapters.
The abridged version contains one hundred thousand verses in forty-eight chapters; having mastered this abridged version by heart, I returned from the Western Regions to my own land.
The transmission of this text to our region consists of eighty fascicles and thirty-nine chapters, which are divided into seven locations and nine assemblies.
Regarding these seven locations and nine assemblies: first, six chapters in eleven fascicles were spoken at the Bodhimaṇḍa;
second, six chapters in four fascicles were spoken in the Hall of Universal Radiance; third, six chapters in three fascicles were spoken in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; fourth, [at] night...
1. *Sūtra Spoken at the Heaven of the Thirty-three*, four chapters, three fascicles; 2. *Sūtra Spoken at the Tuṣita Heaven*, three chapters, twelve fascicles; 3.
*Sūtra Spoken at the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven*, one chapter, six fascicles; 4. *Sūtra Spoken at the Reassembled Universal Radiance Hall*, eleven chapters, thirteen fascicles; 5.
*Sūtra Spoken at the Third Assembly in the Universal Radiance Hall*, one chapter, seven fascicles; 6. *Sūtra Spoken at the Jeta Grove*, [one chapter].
The *Lín Shuō Jīng Yī Pǐn* (One Chapter on the Forest Preaching the Sūtra) in twenty-one fascicles is the lower version of the first division, consisting of thirty-six thousand verses;

there remain sixty-four thousand verses in nine chapters still extant in the Western Regions. Although the sūtra is not yet complete, the intent of the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*dharmadeśanā*), and the dissemination (*pariṇāmana*) is already fully prepared.
How is this known? National Teacher Qingliang judged the five-fascicle sūtra to be the introductory division (*nidāna-bhāga*).
The first fifteen volumes and a half constitute the *Zhengzongfen* (Section on the Main Doctrine); the remaining nineteen volumes and a half constitute the *Liutongfen* (Section on Circulation).

The *Xingyuanpin* (Chapter on Vows and Practices) constitutes a separate circulation. Regarding the title *Dafangguang Fo Huayan Jing*: "Great" (*Da*) is named according to its essential nature, meaning "eternal and pervasive.

"Eternal" signifies vertically exhausting the three periods of time; "pervasive" signifies horizontally encompassing the ten directions. "Fang" (Square/Correct) is named according to the Dharma it accords with.

Its meaning consists of "normative guidance" (*niyama*) and "sustenance" (*dhāraṇa*). "Normative guidance" refers to the rules that give rise to understanding; "sustenance" refers to maintaining one's own nature. It is named extensively according to its functions:
"encompassing" (*saṃgraha*) and "vastness" (*vistara*). "Encompassing" means broad inclusion; "vastness" means universal pervasion.

It is named after the Buddha as a person: "awakening" (*bodha*) and "illumination" (*dyotana*). "Awakening" refers to realizing the profound darkness of the great night; "illumination" refers to clarifying the hidden depths of the myriad phenomena.

The term "flower" (*puṣpa*) is designated by way of analogy; its meaning consists of bringing forth fruit and adorning the body. Regarding the bringing forth of fruit, it signifies the perfect completion of the myriad practices, just as peach and plum flowers are followed by their fruit.
Regarding the adorning of the body, it signifies the fullness of all virtues within one's person, just as gold and jade are beautiful.

While the flower possesses only the sense of adorning the body and lacks the sense of producing fruit, "adornment" (*śobhā*) is designated by way of its function, and its meaning is that of providing resources for ornamentation. As for "providing resources" (*upakaraṇa*), it means—

The title *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* is established as follows: "Great" (*mahā*) refers to its vast essence and function; "Vaipulya" signifies that which is majestic, the true and responsive Buddha-body, and that which is designated by words as its means of expression.

"Sūtra" has the meaning of "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) and "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*). "Gathering" refers to the infinite gathering of sentient beings; "upholding" refers to the inexhaustible upholding of their nature and characteristics.
Therefore, it is named the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*. Furthermore, "Great" is the essence of Vairocana, and "Vaipulya" is Vairocana’s...
That mark is the vastness of Vairocana’s function; the Buddha is Vairocana Buddha, and the flower belongs to Samantabhadra, representing Great Practice;

the adornment belongs to Mañjuśrī, representing Great Wisdom. The profound meaning clarifies that if one wishes to attain Buddhahood, one must first employ the Great Wisdom of Mañjuśrī to mobilize the Great Practice of Samantabhadra to adorn the essential body of the fruit-stage of Vairocana Buddha.

Because it possesses great characteristics, great functions, and greatness, it is called the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*. Furthermore, the character "Great" (*mahā*) corresponds to the Dharma-body;
the character "Vast" (*vaipulya*) corresponds to the Wisdom-body, the Emanation-body, and the Mind-made body; the character "Buddha" corresponds to the Bodhi-body and the Majestic Power-body;
the character "Flower" (*avatamsaka*) corresponds to the Merit-body and the Vow-body; and the character "Adornment" (*sūtra*) corresponds to the adornment of the primary and secondary marks.
Regarding the title *The Great Vaipulya Buddha-Flower Adornment Sūtra, Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Ruler*:

"World" (*loka*) refers to the threefold world—namely, the world of sentient beings, the world of the vessel (the physical environment), and the world of perfect enlightenment—as explained in the sūtra.
It refers to the immeasurable kings of asuras, the immeasurable great dragon kings, the son of the sun deity, and so forth.
These are the lords of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), as exemplified by the mountain deities, forest deities, tree deities, wind deities, river deities, and so forth.

These are the lords of the container world (*bhājana-loka*), as exemplified by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Ratnajvālā-suvimalaprabha Bodhisattva, Mahāpuṇyaprabhāsa-jñānasaṃbhava Bodhisattva, Mahātejaḥ-svararāja Bodhisittva, and others. This is the world of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha-loka*).
The Lord [is adorned by] the sentient world, the vessel world, and the world of perfect enlightenment;
the vessel world adorns the sentient world, and the world of perfect enlightenment adorns both the vessel world and the sentient world.

Because these three worlds mutually adorn one another and are thus called "sublime," it is titled the "Chapter on the Sublime Adornment of the World-Lord" (Lokeshvararajavyuha). Furthermore, the second...

The first assembly expounds the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Primary and Secondary Retributions (the primary retribution being one's own body and the secondary retribution being the dwelling where one resides).

The second assembly expounds the Ten Faiths; the third assembly expounds the Ten Abidings; the fourth assembly expounds the Ten Practices; the fifth assembly expounds the Ten Transferences; the sixth assembly expounds the Ten Grounds;
and the seventh assembly expounds Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment. These seven preceding assemblies are all sequential.

The first teaching is called the Dharma-gate of Sequential Arrangement (*xingbu*). The eighth and ninth assemblies consist of two hundred questions arising from the clouds of universal wisdom and two thousand answers poured forth from the vase of Samantabhadra;
these explain that when a single dharma is taught, all dharmas are contained therein—this is called the Dharma-gate of Perfect Interfusion (*yuanrong*).
Sequential arrangement is like the peach and plum blossoms, where the flowers come first and the fruit follows; perfect interfusion is like... [the text continues].

Regarding the simultaneous perfection of the lotus flower and its fruit through the principle of perfect interfusion (*yūngyōng*), there are two further meanings: first, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruits;

second, the fruit penetrates to the source of the cause. "The cause encompasses the ocean of fruits" means that the ten stages of faith (*shin*), the ten abodes (*ju*), the ten practices (*gyō*), the ten transferences (*ekō*), the ten grounds (*jichi*), equal enlightenment (*tōkaku*), and wondrous enlightenment (*myōkaku*) are all contained within it. "The fruit penetrates to the source of the cause" refers to what follows after equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment.
The ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten abodes (*vihāra*), and the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) are all contained within this.

Therefore it is said: in terms of sequential arrangement (*pratipatti-vyavasthāna*), the characteristics of the teachings are distinct; yet in terms of perfect interfusion (*yuganaddha*), essence and characteristics are without obstruction.

Because characteristics are precisely the characteristics of essence, sequential arrangement does not obstruct perfect interfusion. Because essence is precisely the essence of characteristics, perfect interfusion does not obstruct sequential arrangement. Perfect interfusion is round.
Because fusion does not obstruct sequential manifestation, the one becomes the immeasurable; because sequential manifestation does not obstruct fusion, the immeasurable becomes the one.
When the immeasurable is the one, they are fused and interpenetrating; when the one is the immeasurable, they enter into one another in layers.
Furthermore, the structural format of this sutra’s movement proceeds from the great to the small, as the opening of the sutra states: "At that time, the World-Honored One..."
In the Bodhimaṇḍa of the forest retreats in the kingdom of Magadha, he attained the wisdom of supreme perfect enlightenment regarding all phenomena;
his realization entered into the equality of the three periods of time; his body pervaded all worlds;
his voice universally accorded with the lands of the ten directions, like space containing all forms; and he remained undivided amidst all objective realms.
Apart from this, there is the great opening that swallows the worlds of the ten directions in a single gulp.
If one has not yet attained such a realization, one must gradually narrow the scope to accommodate others:

using the eleven fascicles of the sutra to open the gate of faith for sentient beings, the forty-one fascicles to open the gate of understanding for sentient beings, and the seven fascicles to open [the gate of practice] for sentient beings.
The twenty-one fascicles of the *Jing* (Sūtra) issued as a gate for the sake of sentient beings constitute a single treatise on the gates of cultivation and realization.

This scripture does not transcend the four gates of faith (*śraddhā*), understanding (*adhimukti*), practice (*pratipatti*), and realization (*adhigama*). These are the teachings that express [the truth] (*vyañjana*).

As for the meanings expressed (*artha*) therein, they do not transcend the four divisions, the five periods, the six characteristics, the ten mysteries, the four kinds of dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), the twenty layers of the Flower Treasury (*puṣpakaraṇḍaka*), and the non-... [omitted].

Regarding the fourfold division of the ocean of fragrant water: first, the section on manifesting the fruit and encouraging joy to give rise to faith; second, the section on cultivating the causes to accord with the fruit and give rise to understanding;
third, the section on relying on the Dharma to advance in cultivation and accomplish practice; and fourth, the section on relying on persons to enter into realization and accomplish virtue.

As for the five cycles: the eleven fascicles of the sutra belong to the cycle of the cause and fruit to be believed; the forty-one fascicles of the preceding sutra belong to the cycle of differentiation.
The Cycle of Distinct Causes and Effects consists of the *Seven-Scroll Sūtra*; the Cycle of Equal Causes and Effects consists of the *Twenty-One-Scroll Sūtra*;

and the Cycle of Causes and Effects for Realization and Entry consists of the *Six Characteristics*. As for these six characteristics, they are: the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the identical characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*), the different characteristic (*visama-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of formation (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of destruction (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*). To explain them by way of analogy: the "general" is like a single person, who is called the "general aspect."

The distinctness of each part, such as the feet and head, is called their "distinct characteristic" (*biphasa*). The fact that the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, and feet together constitute a single body is called their "common characteristic" (*sāmānyalaksana*).

The fact that their functions differ—such as the eye requiring sight, the ear requiring sound, the tongue requiring taste, the nose requiring fragrance, the hand requiring grasping, and the foot requiring running—is called their "different characteristic" (*viśeṣalaksana*).
The eighty-four thousand pores being completed all at once is called... [the "simultaneous characteristic"].
Regarding the characteristics of completion (*chengxiang*): the head must point upward and the feet must point downward; the eyebrows must be above the eyes and the ears on both sides;

they must not be disordered but each occupy its own position—this is called the characteristic of integrity (*huaixiang*). Next, as for the explanation of the Dharma (*fashe*), the eighty fascicles of the sutra belong to the general characteristic (*zongxiang*);

the textual content of each individual fascicle is distinct, which is called the specific characteristic (*biexiang*); and that which constitutes the entirety of this one sutra is called... [the characteristic of totality].

The eleven fascicles of the *Tongxiang jing* (Sūtra of Identical Characteristics) primarily open up faith; the forty-one fascicles of the *Yao kaishe jing* (Essential Sūtra Opening Understanding) primarily open up understanding;

the seven fascicles of the *Yao kexing jing* (Essential Sūtra Opening Practice) primarily open up practice; and the twenty-one fascicles of the *Yao kezeng gongyong jing* (Essential Sūtra Opening Realization of Function) each have distinct functions, which are termed "Diverse Characteristics" (*yixiang*).

The eighty fascicles of the *Chengxiang jing* (Sūtra of Accomplished Characteristics) achieve perfection in every single fascicle, which is termed "Accomplished Characteristics" (*chengxiang*). The first fascicle of this sūtra must not be placed at the beginning.
The second fascicle of the sutra may not follow after the third fascicle; the former may not be after the latter, and the latter may not be before the former.

Each returns to its original position upon being rearranged. This is what is meant by "this dharma abides in its dharma-position, and the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding"—this is called the characteristic of rearrangement (*huài-xiàng*).
Next, as for the ten mysteries (*shí xuán*), the first is simultaneous and complete mutual correspondence (*tóng-shí jù-zú xiāng-yìng*).

1. The Gate of the Flavor of the Ocean Containing the Tastes of All Rivers; 2. The Gate of the Unobstructed Sovereignty of the Broad and the Narrow (a one-foot mirror reflecting a thousand layers of images); 3.

The Gate of the Mutual Interpenetration of the One and the Many Without Confusion (the light of a single lamp in a room entering into every other light); 4. The Gate of the Sovereign Identity of All Dharmas (like gold and its color, which are inseparable); 5.

The Gate of the Simultaneous Accomplishment of the Secret, the Hidden, and the Manifest (a crescent moon in a clear sky where darkness and light coexist); 6. The Gate of the Subtle Interpenetration and Stable Establishment of All Things.

1. The Gate of the Door (like a lapis lazuli vase containing many mustard seeds); 2. The Gate of the Realm of the Seven Indra-nets (two mirrors reflecting each other, their radiance pouring into one another); 3.

The Gate of Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena to Generate Understanding (erecting images and raising arms—everything before the eyes is the Way); 4. The Gate of the Ten Worlds Being Distinct Yet Accomplishing One Another (a single night’s dream spanning a hundred years); 5.

The Gate of the Principal and its Associates Being Perfectly Radiant and Endowed with Virtue (the North Star, where all the stars bow). The essential meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is contained herein.
On a single atom, the six aspects and ten mysteries are clarified; next, regarding the four kinds of *dharmadhātu*, Master Guifeng said:

"Because the principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) have not yet been fully elucidated, nor emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*), one points directly to the numinous source of original enlightenment; therefore, it is called the 'One True *Dharmadhātu*'.

From this One True *Dharmadhātu* are differentiated the *Dharmadhātu* of Principle, the *Dharmadhātu* of Phenomena, the *Dharmadhātu* of the Unobstructed Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena, and the *Dharmadhātu* of Phenomena...

The dharma-realm of non-obstruction of phenomena takes "normative rules" as its meaning, while the realm takes "differentiation of nature" as its meaning. This dharma of the normative rules of true emptiness is the principle-dharma-realm when considered from the perspective of principle;

it is the phenomenon-dharma-realm when considered from the perspective of phenomena; it is the dharma-realm of non-obstruction between principle and phenomena when considered from the perspective of both principle and phenomena;
and it is the dharma-realm of non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena when considered from the perspective of phenomena alone. This is because principle is without differentiation.
Limitations and phenomena differ in a thousand ways. An ancient poem says: "The spring colors have no high or low; the flowering branches have their short and long.

This is just as it is said in the sutras: there is a wise person (the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas) who breaks open a single atom (the two attachments to self and dharmas within the body of an ordinary being) and brings forth a great scroll (the principle-dharmadhātu), upon which are written the events of the three-thousandfold great chiliocosm (the phenomenon-dharmadhātu, the non-obstruction of principle and phenomenon, and the non-obstruction of phenomenon and phenomenon).

The obstructed *dharmadhātu*. Next, regarding the twentyfold *puṣpagañja* worlds: the first ten layers represent self-benefit (*svārtha*), and the latter ten layers represent benefit for others (*parārtha*).

The fact that Vairocana Buddha resides in the thirteenth layer represents the urgency of his mind to benefit others. Furthermore, it must be understood that there are ten locations from which light is emitted;
at the initial site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there are two [initial points]: first, light is emitted from the face (*mukha-dvāra*), representing the teaching (*deśanā*).
1. Because the Way extends afar, light is emitted from between the eyebrows next, universally manifesting the Middle Way of the One Vehicle. 2.

In the Hall of Universal Radiance, light is emitted from the wheels of the feet, signifying the foundation of the initial practice of faith. 3. In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, light is emitted from the toes of the feet, signifying abiding securely.
4. In the Yāma Heaven, light is emitted from above the feet, signifying reliance upon practice. 5. In the Tuṣita Heaven, [light is emitted] from the knees.
1. The wheel emitting light symbolizes the dedication of merit through the bending and extending [of the limbs]. 2.

The sixth [assembly], where the Heavens of Making Use of Others' Transformations emit light from between the eyebrows, symbolizes the realization of the Middle Way within the ten suchnesses. 3. The seventh [assembly] in the Universal Radiance Hall has two parts:

first, the emission of light from between the eyebrows symbolizes non-abiding in the two extremes of birth-and-death and nirvana; second, the emission of light from the mouth symbolizes that Samantabhadra is born from the Buddha’s mouth.
The first assembly was held at the Jeta Grove; the light emitted from between the eyebrows signifies the realization of the Middle Way that exhausts the entire Dharma-realm.

As for the third assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsamaṇḍapa*), no light was emitted because practice depends upon understanding; it signifies the manifestation of light solely through the arising of understanding.
Furthermore, each of the nine assemblies has its own presiding figure: the first assembly is presided over by Samantabhadra, and the second assembly by Mañjuśrī (in this sutra, it is Samantabhadra).
For the eldest son Mañjuśrī and the youngest son [it is as follows]: The Third Assembly is Dharmamati; the Fourth Assembly is Guṇakara;

the Fifth Assembly is Vajradhvaja; the Sixth Assembly is Vajragarbha; and the Seventh Assembly is Samantabhadra. In the "Chapter on the Universal Good" (Samantabhadra-parivarta), the equality of the cause is discussed;
in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," the equality of the fruit is discussed. The Eighth Assembly is again Samantabhadra, and the Ninth Assembly is likewise.

Regarding the Tathāgata’s association with spiritual friends: furthermore, among the thirty-nine chapters, only the "A-saṃkhyeya" chapter and the "Tathāgata-anuvyañjana-prabhāsa" chapter were spoken by the Buddha (these two chapters are dharma-gates personally realized by the Buddha);
all other chapters were expounded by various Bodhisattvas and the Jewel-Network of the Cloud-Pavilion, while the Buddha merely emitted light. The many meanings thus elucidated are complete.
From the boundless ocean of fragrant water, an infinite ocean of fragrant water flows forth; furthermore, from a single mind, its subsequent [emanations] flow forth.
Then, at the eastern edge of the City of Blessings (*Puṇyavatī*), before a great stūpa, the youth Sudhana beheld Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī manifested as an elephant king looking back, letting out a lion’s roar and a yawn. At that moment, six thousand bhikṣus attained realization upon hearing these words.
The Way and the five aggregates are beneficial friends that suddenly awaken the initial mind. When Sudhana attained realization, Mañjuśrī told him:
"Now that you have seen me, you have obtained fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), yet you have not yet obtained discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

You may travel south [the South being the realm of empty luminosity, which is one's own self] and pass through one hundred and ten cities to visit fifty-three virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), examining each of their distinct gateways."
The *Song of Chan Master Chengdengzhengjue of Foguo* says: "Leaving the forest only to enter it again—this is the Buddha-temple at Sāla.
When the lion roars toward the east, the fragrant grasses are green; As the Elephant King looks back, the fallen blossoms are red. The six thousand mendicants have fulfilled their ten minds;
The eminent ones among the five assemblies have attained penetration through a single faith. Take care, my teacher, as you head south."
"Passing through a hundred cities, the misty waters stretch out infinitely. Thereupon, Sudhana took leave of Mañjuśrī and ascended Mount Sumeru to seek the Bhikṣu Meghashvara.
He circumambulated the mountain for seven days without seeing him, until later he met him on a different peak.
This Mount Sumeru is the ultimate point; throughout the entirety of the ten directions, there is but this single Mount Sumeru. This is why Sudhana...
If one does not see [the Master], yet there must be seeing, hearing, speaking, and listening—setting aside this, the "separate peaks" (bie feng) refers to the head of the second stage.
Furthermore, the verse says: "Guṇabhadra always dwells on the peak of Mount Sumeru; he circumambulates the summit, his tracks never fixed.
Though sought for seven days, he cannot be found; why then do they meet again in a single morning? This is the Master’s place where he resolved his mind.

The gate of universal vision through the convergence of conditions (the stage of "Generating the Mind") reveals the Buddha-realm within its expanse (Sudhana attains the Dharma-gate of Universal Vision).
Turning his head to gaze down the slope of the setting sun, he beholds thousands upon thousands of layers of white clouds and blue peaks. Sudhana takes his leave and travels south;
wherever he encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), each says: "I have already first generated the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know [how to fulfill it]..."

What kind of practice does Sudhana cultivate, and how does he resolve his mind? First presenting what has already been resolved and subsequently inquiring about the gates of practice is precisely the sequence of first awakening and then cultivating.

Within this interval, for instance, when he sees the Brahmin Śroṇa Kotīviṃśa amidst four masses of fire with a mountain of swords rising steeply and boundlessly in their midst, Sudhana climbs the mountain and leaps into the fire, thereby attaining the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Wheel and becoming a prince.
This is indeed an adverse circumstance. Master Zhong composed a verse on it, saying: "The youth sought out the master Śaṇṭha; The gate of his teaching revealed a unique style.
Only after climbing the mountain of blades and leaping into the mass of fire Did he suddenly awaken to the perfection of luminosity, realizing that form is emptiness.
It is like seeing King Anala seated upon the vajra throne, Surrounded before and behind by ten thousand ministers and one hundred thousand [attendants]."
The fierce soldiers were hideous in appearance; they all bared their arms and glared with fury. Those whom they had violated had their hands and feet severed, or their ears and noses cut off.
Once the King had finished his affairs of state, he took Sudhana by the hand, entered the palace, and commanded him to sit together with him.
Seeing that the palace was vast and expansive, composed entirely of exquisite jewels, the King said to Sudhana: "I have attained the dharma of illusion."
That his actions of body, speech, and mind never once troubled a single sentient being was also an adverse condition. Master Zhong composed a verse on this:
"The King’s majesty is stern, the jailer is wrathful; To have one's heart, arms, and belly carved out is most distressing.

Yet as he is led with hesitation into the Hall of Non-arising, A single song sounds in the peach and plum blossoms of the rear garden. It was also like seeing the house where the woman Vasumitrā dwelt.
Extensive, magnificent, and beautiful, the jeweled trees, jeweled walls, and jeweled moats were each adorned with ten great gardens that graced her body.
Emanating great radiance that universally illuminated all the palaces, she would sometimes hold, embrace, kiss, or sip [the youth], whereby he attained refreshing coolness.
She said to Sudhana: "I have attained the dharma-gate called 'The Limit Beyond Greed.'"
Chan Master Fokuo composed this verse: Meeting and greeting, what karmic affinity do we share? The Tathāgata of Noble Conduct offers a single precious coin.
Holding hands and embracing, the moon in the heart-mind is serene; Kissing and caressing, the pearl of precepts is perfect. Humans, non-humans, and women all appear in succession;
Heavenly beings and celestial forms respond without partiality. The three virtues are already manifest at the limit of desire; In the wine tower and flowery grotto, one is intoxicated.

The Immortals and Transcendents follow next; together they appear as the Youth Virtue-Born (Guṇākara) and the Maiden Virtuous (Guṇavatī). The male represents wisdom and the female represents compassion.
Regarding the term "child" (tóng), it signifies freedom from defiled habits. Master Zhōng composed a verse on this:

"The boy and the girl, their bones and flesh fresh, Lead each other by hand, holding a jade qílín. They come with earnest intent to inform Sudhana: 'The road before Maitreya’s tower is most intimate.'"
Furthermore, the *Buddhakṣetragāthā* says: "Guṇākara and Guṇavatī, in harmonious union, Are alike in illusion and alike in intention, their purpose inexhaustible.
Abiding together and practicing together, they achieve liberation; Sharing compassion and wisdom, they manifest spiritual power. Sharing virtue and sharing thought, their minds are in secret accord;
Sharing vision and sharing knowledge, the Way flows through them. If you wish to attain the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime, The Vairocana pavilion lies to the south."

Thereupon, Sudhana paid his respects and took leave, proceeding to the terrace of Maitreya where he prostrated and said, "I only pray that the Venerable One will open the door of this pavilion so that I may enter.

At that moment, Maitreya led forth immeasurable great bodhisattvas who had come from other directions—symbolizing that all phenomena have no fixed abode—and with a single snap of his fingers—symbolizing non-separation from one's current location—the door of the pavilion opened. Sudhana immediately entered; having entered, [he beheld...]
Furthermore, [the gates] are closed (symbolizing the gathering of functions back into the essence, and indicating that the gates of phenomenal expression are transcended).
Sudhana beholds a single pavilion, vast and inexhaustible like space; he further sees within this pavilion countless wondrous pavilions, and within each of these pavilions there is Maitreya.
Before each Maitreya stands Sudhana, and all these Sudhanas are joined together as one.
The palms turned back to look at the body of a single Sudhana, which entered into the interior of all the bodies of Sudhana;
all the bodies of Sudhana were gathered and returned into the interior of the body of that single Sudhana.

One pavilion became the sovereign and all the other pavilions became its attendants, mutually pervasive, mutually containing, mutually encompassing, and mutually entering, layer upon layer, infinitely. This is the realization and entry into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The *Foguo Song* (Verses on the Buddha-land) says: Standing for a brief moment before the gate of the pavilion, the teacher of the Dragon Flower returns from afar.

Not only do you contemplate the profound and wondrous by snapping your fingers, but you also hear his compassionate voice speaking with subtle detail. Wisdom, principle, conduct, and action constitute his body;
the sun and moon are the pivot and mechanism of his bodhicitta. From where do these many realms come or go? A single wild goose at ten thousand miles across the sky.
Flying forth, Sudhana attained the liberation door of the "Treasury of Adornments of All Realms.
He thought to himself, "What I have now realized was not achieved without the guidance of Mañjuśrī at the great stupa on the eastern edge of Puṇḍravardhana;
how could I have reached this state otherwise? While he was reflecting thus, Mañjuśrī extended his golden arm across one hundred and ten cities, yet it remained invisible.

In Mañjuśrī’s body, one sees only Mañjuśrī’s hand; (the initial awakening seems to have subject and object, but upon realization, both subject and object vanish. He strokes Sudhana’s crown and says: "Excellent, excellent!
Although your understanding of the Dharma you have realized is already perfected, your practice is not yet perfected.
You should go further to see Samantabhadra; he shall cause you to attain profound and wondrous conduct. Thereupon, Sudhana takes his leave from within the assembly of all Buddhas.

Upon the seat of the red lotus, he beheld Samantabhadra; having perfected the practice of his vows through the fulfillment of wisdom and compassion, he attained samādhis and Dharma-gates as numerous as the atoms within all Buddha-fields.
A verse from the *Buddhakṣetra* states: "One hundred yojanas away, he receives the crown-moistening touch;
In a single thought, he contemplates the presence of the Master Samantabhadra. Majestically manifest upon the red lotus seat, He stands distinct and clear upon the white elephant."

When the wisdom and compassion of the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* were finally fulfilled, and when the vows as numerous as motes of dust in the sunbeams were perfectly completed, the Buddha once again proclaimed the ocean of his merits;
it was sorrowful to see the waves of this teaching rolling out vast and boundless. When Sudhana beheld Mañjuśrī, that was the perfection of understanding (*prajñā*);

when he beheld Samantabhadra, that was the perfection of practice (*caryā*). Since both practice and understanding were perfected, the final verse simply says: "In every thought-moment within atoms of lands..."
One might be able to count and exhaust the waters within the great ocean, measure the void, or bind the wind; yet no one can fully describe the merits of the Buddha.
Having spoken thus, he ceased and never spoke again. One might wonder where Sudhana will attain Buddhahood, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Only upon reaching this point does one come to know that above there is no Buddha-way to be attained, and below there are no sentient beings [to be saved].
"All sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning; birth and death, as well as nirvana, are like a dream from yesterday. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"Even the attainment of the Way involves no acquisition, for the original nature is already perfect and complete. An ancient master said: "In studying the Way, one must first minutely discern the mind.

The most subtle within the subtle is the most difficult to clarify. Only when you search within this until there is nowhere left to find can you truly believe that the ordinary mind is [the Buddha-mind]."
Chan Master Zhongxin of Fosi composed this verse: Beating the drum and playing the pipa, they return to one another as a family.
The wooden boy can clap his hands; the stone woman knows how to brew tea. Clouds disperse to reveal the moon at the edge of the sky; spring comes and flowers bloom upon the trees.
Sudhana traveled everywhere in search of teachers, yet the black bean had not yet sprouted its bud. Therefore, after Zhaozhou had finished his travels and visited all masters, he said, "Buddha..."
I do not like to hear this single word. Layman Zhang Wujin composed a verse on it, saying: "Zhaozhou was eighty years old and still traveling on foot;

it was only because his heart had not yet become tranquil. When he finally completed his universal study and there was not a single thing left, he then knew that he had wasted his straw sandals for nothing.
This is entirely in accord with the meaning of this sutra. I once attended upon Chan Master Zhenxie at the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*’s General Meaning.
Having heard bits and pieces by ear and caught glimpses by eye, I did not dare keep them secret, but have immediately recorded them here to facilitate their wide circulation.
This is "The Master Furan’s Synthesis of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra."
